text: performance criteria. 3.2 Bench-Scale Performance Initial experiments were conducted to characterize plasma ignition, electrical behavior, and gas- phase chemistry under controlled bench-scale conditions. Methane flow rates between 1 and 50 SLPM were regulated using mass-flow controllers. The voltage and current traces were recorded to evaluate instantaneous discharge energy and confirm proper synchronization of pulse timing. At low average power levels (8–20 W), the reformer demonstrated consistent and repeatable plasma formation. Figure 6 shows a representative oscilloscope capture of a single low-power discharge pulse. The yellow trace represents voltage, and the blue trace corresponds to current. The sharp voltage spike followed by a damped decay indicates the rapid establishment of a non- equilibrium discharge. The measured pulse characteristics verified stable plasma operation and confirmed the ability of the pulse-power system to deliver the short, high-voltage bursts required for methane reforming. Figure 6 intentionally omitted from public version. Electrical diagnostics performed during bench-scale testing confirmed stable formation of pulsed, non-thermal plasma discharges across the operating range evaluated. Voltage and current measurements verified consistent pulse initiation, rapid energy coupling to the plasma, and repeatable discharge behavior under steady flow conditions. Detailed waveform data are protected and therefore not included in this public version. Figure 6. Representative low-power pulse waveform recorded during bench-scale plasma reformer operation. The trace shows a voltage spike followed by a rapid current response, confirming stable pulse formation and proper energy coupling between the power driver and discharge gap. Southwest Research Institute® U.S. DOE Award Number DE-FE0032301 Public Version - 6 - DE-FE0032301 Final Report The complete laboratory setup used for these tests is shown in Figure 7. The reformer consisted of a cylindrical plasma zone enclosed in a stainless-steel pressure housing, connected to a high- voltage probe, transformer, and gas-analysis instrumentation. Methane feedstock entered through a metered flow manifold, while exhaust gas was sampled downstream for real-time compositional measurements using a residual gas analyzer. The experimental configuration allowed for precise control of input power, gas flow, and pressure, ensuring reproducibility across multiple test runs. Figure 7. Bench-scale test configuration for plasma reformer performance evaluation. The left image shows the primary electrical components, including transformer, power supplies, and high-voltage probe; the right image shows the downstream exhaust system and gas-analysis instrumentation. When the plasma was energized, the hydrogen fraction in the reformer outlet increased by approximately 1.5 percent at an input power of 20 W, corresponding to a linear yield of 0.075 percent H per watt of electrical power delivered to the reformer. In non-thermal plasmas, electron impact 2 dissociation rates scale roughly linearly with absorbed power. This occurs because electron density and mean electron energy rise proportionally, while gas temperature, residence time, and flow distribution stay relatively constant. Figure 8 shows the projected hydrogen decomposition percentage as a function of power based on these assumptions. This extrapolation indicated that the project’s target decomposition levels (> 20%) could be achieved without major hardware modifications. Figure 8.
